doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: The blues, swing and what counts as jazz
title: Swing, fusion and counterstatement in art
summary: Thomas describes the feeling of swing, his taste for fusion, and how artists define themselves against influences, citing Albert Murray on Baldwin.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Right. And that’s okay. But there are people who get confused. Why do they get confused? Because you have radio stations that were playing things that they called jazz but that really wasn’t jazz. Now you’ve got certain stations that are influenced more, like WRVR in New York in the late 70s that played jazz, what we call jazz, but they also played fusion, which is like a combination of jazz with rock and other elements. Okay. I’m not a purist though. I mean that’s why I say it’s okay if you want to play something else. And also because actually for me, what they call fusion is something that when I first got into the music I loved. And what I would do is I would — because interestingly enough, I don’t think I’ve ever articulated this or written this. But what I used to do is, it was more for swing because I mean man I just love swinging. Because there was something about, because as a player, being in a context where you’re playing in a band and you get a certain groove going, and it just is so uplifting. And when you’re swinging, I mean when you think about the combination of a bass player walking, a drummer riding the cymbal — notice these are movement metaphors — the piano player comping accompanying. And that groove together creates what they call that swing feeling. For a soloist that’s something that you can ride on, that you can fly with, that you can interact with. Maybe you’re going to rub up against it where they’re here and you’re there. It creates this tension and release and this form of expression, this freedom that’s so powerful. So if you are going to not express yourself in that medium and not have elements of the blues, then why would you want to call yourself a jazz musician? Now I’m not saying that there are not elements of the jazz tradition, what I would say is part of the jazz tradition, that counter-stated that, that went another direction where there’s the song form or song stylings there’s a whole part of the music that extended, you know, experimental part and stuff. But they are in part experimenting not only by incorporating other genres of music from classical to other styles, but it’s also a counterstatement to what is that tradition. Which is valid. I mean art is about an expression but it’s also about statement and counterstatement, so that when you as an artist are developing your own identity you incorporate certain people whose style you like or love, and you learn that, and the part of you expressing and becoming into your own and with your own identity, and then some that you don’t like. And as you develop your own style you say well — that influences you too. So I don’t like that. So what I do counters that. I don’t really dig that you know. Or I like this. And that’s just the nature of the way art is. This is not just music. This is in writing too. I once asked Albert Murray if James Baldwin was an influence on him. And he said, “Yes. He was an influence. He influenced me in what not to do.” I’d never thought about it in that way.
Yeah. You can learn something from things you don’t like.
